claim: Ntrk2 (the gene encoding BDNF's receptor TrkB) is in the top 20 of all protein-coding RNAs (#18) in cortical astrocytes from late juvenile (PND 28) mice.
source: Analysis of this sequencing data revealed Ntrk2, the gene encoding BDNF's high affinity receptor TrkB, to be in the top 20 of all protein coding RNA's (#18) detected.
evidence: Based on RNA sequencing data from acutely isolated cortical astrocytes at PND 28.

claim: PND28 astrocytes predominately express the truncated TrkB.T1 isoform, with nearly 90% of all Ntrk2 expression attributed to TrkB.T1.
source: Therefore, isoform-specific transcript expression was assessed and revealed that PND28 astrocytes predominately express the truncated isoform, with nearly 90% of all Ntrk2 expression in cortical astrocytes attributed to TrkB.T1 (151.91 + /- 9.18 FPKM for NM_008745, 19.30 + /- 4.45 FPKM for NM_001025074) (Figure 1B).
evidence: RNA sequencing data showing FPKM values for TrkB.T1 and TrkB.FL isoforms, with Figure 1B displaying the quantification.

claim: Astrocytes express the highest levels of total TrkB mRNA relative to neurons and microglia in PND 28 mice.
source: QPCR analysis of total and isoform-specific Ntrk2 mRNA expression indicated total TrkB (primer detects both isoforms, gray in Figure 1A) was most highly expressed in astrocytes, relative to neurons or microglia.
evidence: qPCR analysis of sequentially isolated cell populations from PND 28 mice, shown in Figure 1C.

claim: TrkB.FL is the predominant isoform expressed by neuronal populations.
source: TrkB.FL is the predominant isoform expressed by neuronal populations (Figure 1D), while astrocytes predominately expressed the truncated TrkB.T1 (Figure 1E).
evidence: qPCR data from isolated cell populations shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Expression of the truncated TrkB.T1 receptor is highest during the juvenile period (PND 28) relative to young (PND 8) and adult (PND 60) astrocytes.
source: QPCR analysis indicated low expression of the full length receptor regardless of time point. In contrast, expression of the truncated receptor was highest during the juvenile period (PND 28, Figure 1F) relative to young (PND 8) and adult (PND 60) astrocytes when total availability of BDNF peaks in the cortex (Figure 1G).
evidence: qPCR analysis across developmental time points shown in Figure 1F and 1G.

claim: The peak expression of TrkB.T1 in astrocytes correlates with the height of astrocyte morphological maturation.
source: Intriguingly, this time period correlates with the height of astrocyte morphological maturation.
evidence: Temporal correlation between TrkB.T1 expression peak and known period of astrocyte morphological maturation.

claim: In vitro astrocytes cultured in serum-free media exhibit TrkB.T1 mRNA levels comparable to age-matched in vivo astrocytes.
source: TrkB mRNA and protein expression was additionally verified, with similar levels of TrkB.T1 mRNA as age-matched in vivo astrocytes (Figure 2C).
evidence: qPCR comparison between cultured and acutely isolated astrocytes shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In vitro astrocytes exhibit a developmental upregulation of TrkB.T1 mRNA at 14DIV, similar to the upregulation seen in juvenile astrocytes.
source: Importantly, in vitro astrocytes exhibited a developmental upregulation of TrkB.T1 mRNA at 14DIV, similar to the upregulation seen juvenile astrocytes.
evidence: qPCR data comparing TrkB.T1 expression at 7DIV and 14DIV in cultured astrocytes shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Culturing astrocytes in serum-free media results in 3.43-fold more complex astrocytes compared to serum-containing media as assessed by Shape Index.
source: Notably, culturing astrocytes in serum free media resulted in 3.43-fold more complex astrocyte as assessed by Shape Index of GFAP immunostained cells (t (198)=13.39, p<0.0001; Figure 2E–F).
evidence: Shape Index quantification comparing serum-free and serum-containing culture conditions shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: Visualization of astrocyte membrane using Glast staining reveals 1.5-fold increased cellular complexity relative to GFAP staining.
source: Unsurprisingly, comparison of Shape index quantification from membrane (Glast) staining revealed a 1.5 fold increased cellular complexity relative to intermediate filaments (GFAP) staining, (t(164) = 4.183, p<0.001; Figure 2E–F).
evidence: Shape Index comparison between Glast and GFAP staining shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: Wildtype astrocytes exposed to 30 ng BDNF for 24 hours show a 2-fold increase in average morphological complexity.
source: Shape Index complexity analysis revealed BDNF-treated astrocytes showed a 2-fold increase in average astrocyte morphological complexity after exposure to 30 ng BDNF (F(3, 214)=7.047; p=0.001; Figure 3A–C).
evidence: Shape Index quantification of astrocytes treated with varying BDNF concentrations shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: Scavenging BDNF with TrkB-Fc inhibits the increase in astrocyte morphological complexity induced by BDNF.
source: SI quantification of cellular complexity 24 hr later demonstrated that scavenging BDNF inhibited the increase in astrocyte morphological complexity (H = 70.41; p=0.98; Figure 3D–F).
evidence: Shape Index analysis of astrocytes treated with BDNF and TrkB-Fc shown in Figure 3D-F.

claim: TrkB.T1 KO astrocytes do not show increased morphological complexity in response to 30 ng BDNF treatment.
source: SI quantification and cumulative frequency analysis revealed no difference in control- and 30ng-treated TrkB.T1 KO astrocyte cellular complexities (F(3, 155) = 21.66, p = 0.39; H (4, 136) =4 0.88, p = 0.99, respectively; Figure 3G–I).
evidence: Shape Index and cumulative frequency analysis of TrkB.T1 KO astrocytes treated with BDNF shown in Figure 3G-I.

claim: BDNF signaling through TrkB.T1 increases astrocyte morphological complexity.
source: Our data, therefore, suggests that BDNF signaling through TrkB.T1 increases astrocyte morphological complexity.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from loss-of-function experiments using TrkB-Fc scavenging and TrkB.T1 KO astrocytes.

claim: Wildtype astrocyte volume increases by 2-fold between PND 14 and PND 28.
source: In line with previous reports, WT astrocyte volume increased by 2-fold between PND 14 and PND 28 (p<0.001), and another 1.3-fold between PND 28 and PND 50 (p = 0.0021) with a total 2.8-fold increase in complexity between PND 14 and PND 50 astrocytes (p = <0.001), indicative of normal morphological maturation (Figure 4C–E) (Bushong et al., 2004; Morel et al., 2014; Stogsdill et al., 2017).
evidence: Imaris surface reconstruction volume quantification across developmental time points shown in Figure 4C-E, with citation to previous literature.

claim: TrkB.T1 KO astrocytes show no significant difference in volume between PND 14 and PND 28.
source: In contrast, this increase in morphogenesis was lost in TrkB.T1 KO animals, with no significant difference between PND 14 and 28 astrocyte volumes (p=0.9996; Figure 4E).
evidence: Volume quantification of TrkB.T1 KO astrocytes across development shown in Figure 4E.

claim: By PND 28, TrkB.T1 KO astrocytes demonstrate a 30% reduction in volume compared to WT littermates.
source: By PND 28, TrkB.T1 KO astrocytes demonstrated a 30% reduction in volume compared to WT littermates (Figure 4C,E; p = 0.003; n = 29 cells from 6 WT animals, n = 27 cells from 7 KO animals).
evidence: Volume quantification comparing WT and TrkB.T1 KO astrocytes at PND 28 shown in Figure 4C and 4E.

claim: The reduction in astrocyte volume in TrkB.T1 KO mice persists into PND 50 animals, with a 20% reduction compared to WT littermates.
source: The reduction in volume persisted into PND 50 animals, with a 20% reduction in volume compared to WT littermates (Figure 4D,E; p = 0.03; n = 21 cells from 5 WT animals, n = 17 cells from 5 KO animals).
evidence: Volume quantification comparing WT and TrkB.T1 KO astrocytes at PND 50 shown in Figure 4D and 4E.

claim: BDNF signaling onto TrkB.T1 in astrocytes is an important pathway for normal astrocyte morphogenesis.
source: Thus, our data suggest that BDNF signaling onto TrkB.T1 in astrocytes is an important pathway for normal astrocyte morphogenesis.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from in vivo morphological analysis of TrkB.T1 KO astrocytes.

claim: TrkB.T1 KO astrocytes exhibit decreased mRNA expression of Kcnj10 (Kir4.1) by 51.6% compared to WT littermates at PND 25.
source: QPCR analysis revealed decreased mRNA expression in specific gene sets differentially regulated in astrocytes during maturation (Clarke et al., 2018): Kcnj10 (Kir4.1; 51.6%, t(4) = 2.943; p=0.04) and Aq4 (Aqp4; 21.7%, t(4) = 2.807; p=0.04), with trending decrease in Slc1a2 (Glt1; 33.1%, t(6) = 2.242; p=0.056) relative to WT littermate controls (Figure 4F).
evidence: qPCR analysis of acutely isolated astrocytes from PND 25 mice shown in Figure 4F, with citation to Clarke et al., 2018.

claim: TrkB.T1 KO astrocytes exhibit decreased mRNA expression of Aq4 (Aqp4) by 21.7% compared to WT littermates at PND 25.
source: QPCR analysis revealed decreased mRNA expression in specific gene sets differentially regulated in astrocytes during maturation (Clarke et al., 2018): Kcnj10 (Kir4.1; 51.6%, t(4) = 2.943; p=0.04) and Aq4 (Aqp4; 21.7%, t(4) = 2.807; p=0.04), with trending decrease in Slc1a2 (Glt1; 33.1%, t(6) = 2.242; p=0.056) relative to WT littermate controls (Figure 4F).
evidence: qPCR analysis of acutely isolated astrocytes from PND 25 mice shown in Figure 4F, with citation to Clarke et al., 2018.

claim: TrkB.T1 KO astrocytes show a trending decrease in Slc1a2 (Glt1) mRNA expression by 33.1% compared to WT littermates at PND 25.
source: QPCR analysis revealed decreased mRNA expression in specific gene sets differentially regulated in astrocytes during maturation (Clarke et al., 2018): Kcnj10 (Kir4.1; 51.6%, t(4) = 2.943; p=0.04) and Aq4 (Aqp4; 21.7%, t(4) = 2.807; p=0.04), with trending decrease in Slc1a2 (Glt1; 33.1%, t(6) = 2.242; p=0.056) relative to WT littermate controls (Figure 4F).
evidence: qPCR analysis of acutely isolated astrocytes from PND 25 mice shown in Figure 4F, with citation to Clarke et al., 2018.

claim: No difference in Gja1 (Cx43) expression was found between TrkB.T1 KO and WT astrocytes at PND 25.
source: Of note, we found no difference in Gja1 expression (Cx43; t(4) = 0.5491, p=0.612) across the two genotypes, in line with previous studies indicating stable expression after p15 in rodents (Aberg et al., 1999; Iacobas et al., 2012; Prime et al., 2000).
evidence: qPCR analysis shown in Figure 4F, with citations to previous literature on Cx43 expression patterns.

claim: In vivo loss of TrkB.T1 results in dysregulated expression of genes associated with mature astrocyte function.
source: Thus, in vivo loss of TrkB.T1 results in dysregulated expression of genes associated with mature astrocyte function.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from qPCR analysis of perisynaptic genes in TrkB.T1 KO astrocytes.

claim: TrkB.T1 KO astrocytes co-cultured with WT neurons exhibit decreased total complexity compared to WT astrocytes co-cultured with WT neurons.
source: Sholl analysis revealed that .T1 KO astrocytes were less complex overall compared to WT astrocytes as assessed by the Glast staining (Figure 5b; F(1, 26)=17.88; p=0.03).
evidence: Sholl analysis of co-cultured astrocytes shown in Figure 5B.

claim: TrkB.T1 KO astrocytes co-cultured with WT neurons exhibit decreased branch complexity compared to WT astrocytes co-cultured with WT neurons.
source: Additionally, .T1 KO astrocytes exhibited decreased branch complexity (Figure 5c; (F1, 18)=10.68; p=0.004) when co-cultured with WT neurons.
evidence: Sholl analysis of Gfap-stained astrocyte branches shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Egfp-Cre+ astrocytes in TrkB.T1 floxed animals exhibit a 20% reduction in volume compared to WT Egfp-Cre+ astrocytes at PND 28.
source: These astrocytes demonstrated a significant 20% reduction in volume compared to WT eGFP+ astrocytes (t(21) = 2.407; p=0.0254; Figure 5E–G).
evidence: Volume quantification of AAV-Cre infected astrocytes in TrkB.T1 floxed mice shown in Figure 5E-G.

claim: Astrocyte-specific conditional knockout of TrkB.T1 results in 85% reduction of TrkB.T1 expression in astrocytes at PND 25-28.
source: QPCR analysis revealed a significant reduction of TrkB.T1 expression in cKO astrocytes (85%; F(1, 10)=12.80; p=0.0021; Figure 5I) in comparison to cWT astrocytes, with no difference in TrkB.T1 expression in neurons (F(1, 10)=12.80; p=0.7372) or microglia.
evidence: qPCR analysis of sequentially isolated cell populations from conditional knockout mice shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Astrocyte-specific conditional knockout astrocytes exhibit a 19% reduction in volume compared to control littermates at PND 28.
source: Surface reconstruction of astrocyte volumes revealed that cKO astrocytes exhibited a significant 19% reduction in astrocyte complexity compared to cWT littermates (t(30) = 2.592; p=0.015; Figure 5M,N).
evidence: Volume quantification of conditional knockout astrocytes shown in Figure 5M and 5N.

claim: Astrocyte-specific conditional knockout animals exhibit decreased expression of Slc1a2 (Glt1) by 25% compared to control littermates at PND 25-28.
source: QPCR analysis revealed significantly reduced expression of the same genes found in the global TrkB.T1 KO mice. Specifically, cKO animals exhibited decreased expression of Slc1a2 (Glt1; 25%; t(8) = 1.919; p=0.01), Kcnj10 (Kir4.1; 35%; t(8) = 2.525; p=0.035), and Aq4 (Aqp4; 44%; t(4) = 5.944; p=0.004) compared to cWT littermates.
evidence: qPCR analysis of cortical tissue from conditional knockout mice shown in Figure 5O.

claim: Astrocyte-specific conditional knockout animals exhibit decreased expression of Kcnj10 (Kir4.1) by 35% compared to control littermates at PND 25-28.
source: QPCR analysis revealed significantly reduced expression of the same genes found in the global TrkB.T1 KO mice. Specifically, cKO animals exhibited decreased expression of Slc1a2 (Glt1; 25%; t(8) = 1.919; p=0.01), Kcnj10 (Kir4.1; 35%; t(8) = 2.525; p=0.035), and Aq4 (Aqp4; 44%; t(4) = 5.944; p=0.004) compared to cWT littermates.
evidence: qPCR analysis of cortical tissue from conditional knockout mice shown in Figure 5O.

claim: Astrocyte-specific conditional knockout animals exhibit decreased expression of Aq4 (Aqp4) by 44% compared to control littermates at PND 25-28.
source: QPCR analysis revealed significantly reduced expression of the same genes found in the global TrkB.T1 KO mice. Specifically, cKO animals exhibited decreased expression of Slc1a2 (Glt1; 25%; t(8) = 1.919; p=0.01), Kcnj10 (Kir4.1; 35%; t(8) = 2.525; p=0.035), and Aq4 (Aqp4; 44%; t(4) = 5.944; p=0.004) compared to cWT littermates.
evidence: qPCR analysis of cortical tissue from conditional knockout mice shown in Figure 5O.

claim: Loss of the TrkB.T1 receptor in astrocytes, in an otherwise normal environment, results in reduced astrocyte morphogenesis and aberrant gene expression.
source: Thus, our data combined demonstrate that loss of the TrkB.T1 receptor in astrocytes, in an otherwise normal environment, results in reduced astrocyte morphogenesis and aberrant gene expression.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from co-culture experiments, AAV-mediated deletion, and conditional knockout experiments.

claim: Wildtype astrocytes increase excitatory synapse numbers in co-cultured neurons compared to neurons cultured alone.
source: Puncta Analysis quantification of colocalization of pre- and post-synapses (Ippolito and Eroglu, 2010; Stogsdill et al., 2017) revealed that, as expected, excitatory synapse numbers were increased in the presence of WT astrocytes (F(2, 121)=45.19, p<0.001; n = 39 cells None, n = 48 cells WT from N = 6 cultures) which did not occur in the presence of TrkB.T1 KO astrocytes (F(2, 121)=45.19, p=0.1542; n = 43 cells from N = 6 cultures; Figure 6B–D).
evidence: Puncta analysis of VGlut1+/PSD95+ colocalization in neuron-astrocyte co-cultures shown in Figure 6B-D, with citations to methods.

claim: TrkB.T1 KO astrocytes do not increase excitatory synapse numbers in co-cultured neurons compared to neurons cultured alone.
source: Puncta Analysis quantification of colocalization of pre- and post-synapses (Ippolito and Eroglu, 2010; Stogsdill et al., 2017) revealed that, as expected, excitatory synapse numbers were increased in the presence of WT astrocytes (F(2, 121)=45.19, p<0.001; n = 39 cells None, n = 48 cells WT from N = 6 cultures) which did not occur in the presence of TrkB.T1 KO astrocytes (F(2, 121)=45.19, p=0.1542; n = 43 cells from N = 6 cultures; Figure 6B–D).
evidence: Puncta analysis of VGlut1+/PSD95+ colocalization in neuron-astrocyte co-cultures shown in Figure 6B-D, with citations to methods.

claim: Neurons co-cultured with TrkB.T1 KO astrocytes demonstrate reduced mEPSC frequency compared to neurons co-cultured with WT astrocytes.
source: In comparison to neurons co-cultured with WT astrocytes, neurons co-cultured with .T1 KO astrocytes demonstrated a reduced frequency (KS = 0.0456; p<0.001; n = 21 cells WT, n = 24 cells KO from N = 3 cultures; Figure 6G) but increased amplitude (KS = 0.116; p<0.0001; n = 21 cells WT, n = 24 cells KO from N = 3 cultures; Figure 6H).
evidence: Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings of mEPSCs shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Neurons co-cultured with TrkB.T1 KO astrocytes demonstrate increased mEPSC amplitude compared to neurons co-cultured with WT astrocytes.
source: In comparison to neurons co-cultured with WT astrocytes, neurons co-cultured with .T1 KO astrocytes demonstrated a reduced frequency (KS = 0.0456; p<0.001; n = 21 cells WT, n = 24 cells KO from N = 3 cultures; Figure 6G) but increased amplitude (KS = 0.116; p<0.0001; n = 21 cells WT, n = 24 cells KO from N = 3 cultures; Figure 6H).
evidence: Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings of mEPSCs shown in Figure 6H.

claim: TrkB.T1 astrocytes do not support normal excitatory synaptic development and function.
source: These studies suggest, at least in a simple model system, TrkB.T1 astrocytes do not support normal excitatory synaptic development and function.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from synapse quantification and electrophysiology experiments in co-cultures.

claim: Astrocyte maturation in the rodent cortex takes place largely during the first 2–4 postnatal weeks.
source: In the rodent cortex, astrocyte maturation takes place largely during the first 2–4 postnatal weeks.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about astrocyte development timeline.

claim: Immature astrocytes elaborate their processes and infiltrate the neuropil with fine, terminal, leaflet processes during morphological maturation.
source: Importantly, this includes morphological maturation wherein immature astrocytes elaborate their processes and infiltrate the neuropil with fine, terminal, leaflet processes (Bushong et al., 2004).
evidence: Description of astrocyte morphological maturation with citation to Bushong et al., 2004.

claim: A single mature rodent astrocyte encompasses between 20,000–80,000 µM3 of domain space.
source: Underscoring the morphological complexity of these cells, estimates indicate a single mature rodent astrocyte encompasses between 20,000–80,000 µM3 of domain space (Bushong et al., 2002; Halassa et al., 2007), associates with 300–600 neuronal dendrites (Halassa et al., 2007), and contacts more than 100,000 individual synapses (Freeman, 2010).
evidence: Statement of established measurements with citations to Bushong et al., 2002 and Halassa et al., 2007.

claim: A single mature rodent astrocyte associates with 300–600 neuronal dendrites.
source: Underscoring the morphological complexity of these cells, estimates indicate a single mature rodent astrocyte encompasses between 20,000–80,000 µM3 of domain space (Bushong et al., 2002; Halassa et al., 2007), associates with 300–600 neuronal dendrites (Halassa et al., 2007), and contacts more than 100,000 individual synapses (Freeman, 2010).
evidence: Statement of established measurements with citation to Halassa et al., 2007.

claim: A single mature rodent astrocyte contacts more than 100,000 individual synapses.
source: Underscoring the morphological complexity of these cells, estimates indicate a single mature rodent astrocyte encompasses between 20,000–80,000 µM3 of domain space (Bushong et al., 2002; Halassa et al., 2007), associates with 300–600 neuronal dendrites (Halassa et al., 2007), and contacts more than 100,000 individual synapses (Freeman, 2010).
evidence: Statement of established measurements with citation to Freeman, 2010.

claim: The maturation period of astrocyte morphogenesis coincides with neuronal synaptic refinement.
source: The maturation period of astrocyte morphogenesis coincides with neuronal synaptic refinement (Freeman, 2010; Morel et al., 2014) and differential expression of key genes associated with mature astrocyte functions, such as Slc1a2 (Glt1), Kcnj10 (Kir4.1), and Aq4 (Aqp4) (Clarke et al., 2018; Molofsky and Deneen, 2015; Molofsky et al., 2012; Morel et al., 2014; Nwaobi et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement of temporal correlation with citations to Freeman, 2010 and Morel et al., 2014.

claim: Three mechanisms have been identified for astrocyte morphogenesis: FGF/Heartless signaling, glutamate/mGluR5 signaling, and contact-mediated neurexin/neuroligin.
source: To date, three mechanisms have been identified: Fibroblast Growth Factor (FGF)/Heartless signaling (Stork et al., 2014), glutamate/mGluR5 signaling (Morel et al., 2014), and contact-mediated neurexin/neuroligin (Stogsdill et al., 2017).
evidence: Summary of known mechanisms with citations to Stork et al., 2014, Morel et al., 2014, and Stogsdill et al., 2017.

claim: BDNF is a critical growth factor in the development, maturation, and maintenance of the CNS.
source: Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) is a critical growth factor in the development, maturation, and maintenance of the CNS.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about BDNF function.

claim: BDNF's role in neuronal cell growth, differentiation, morphology, and synaptogenesis via TrkB receptor signaling is well characterized.
source: Its role in neuronal cell growth, differentiation, morphology, and synaptogenesis via TrkB receptor signaling is well characterized (Autry and Monteggia, 2012; Fenner, 2012; Park and Poo, 2013).
evidence: Statement of established knowledge with citations to Autry and Monteggia, 2012, Fenner, 2012, and Park and Poo, 2013.

claim: TrkB has two main isoforms in the CNS: the full-length receptor TrkB.FL and the truncated receptor TrkB.T1.
source: In the CNS, TrkB has two main isoforms. The full-length receptor, TrkB.FL, possesses a tyrosine kinase domain that autophosphorylates with BDNF binding, and a truncated receptor, TrkB.T1.
evidence: Description of TrkB isoforms based on established knowledge.

claim: TrkB.T1 lacks the canonical tyrosine kinase domain but BDNF binding to this receptor is thought to signal through a RhoGTPase inhibitor and the phospholipase C (PLC) pathway.
source: While TrkB.T1 lacks the canonical tyrosine kinase domain, BDNF binding to this receptor is thought to signal through a RhoGTPase inhibitor and the phospholipase C (PLC) pathway (Deinhardt and Chao, 2014; Fenner, 2012).
evidence: Description of TrkB.T1 signaling mechanisms with citations to Deinhardt and Chao, 2014 and Fenner, 2012.

claim: Dysregulation of BDNF/TrkB signaling has been implicated in multiple neurological and neurodevelopmental disorders.
source: Dysregulation of BDNF/TrkB signaling has been implicated in multiple neurological and neurodevelopmental disorders (Bolaños and Nestler, 2004; Merighi et al., 2008; Park and Poo, 2013).
evidence: Statement of established knowledge with citations to Bolaños and Nestler, 2004, Merighi et al., 2008, and Park and Poo, 2013.

claim: A role for BDNF in the developmental maturation of astrocytes has not been investigated prior to this study.
source: However, a role for BDNF in the developmental maturation of astrocytes has not been investigated.
evidence: Statement identifying a gap in the literature.

claim: This is the first demonstration that BDNF is involved in the maturation of a non-neuronal cell type.
source: Herein we have demonstrated for the first time that BDNF is involved in the maturation of a non-neuronal cell type.
evidence: Statement of novelty of the findings.

claim: BDNF/TrkB.T1 signaling is a novel unexplored pathway in the role of astrocytes in synapse development.
source: Our studies suggest that BDNF/TrkB.T1 signaling is a novel unexplored pathway in the role of astrocytes in synapse development.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from synapse development experiments.

claim: Astrocyte BDNF/TrkB.T1 signaling may contribute to neurodevelopmental disorders in which BDNF signaling is implicated.
source: Given the role of aberrant synapse development in neurological dysfunction, our results herein suggest astrocyte BDNF/TrkB.T1 signaling may contribute to neurodevelopmental disorders in which BDNF signaling is implicated.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential clinical implications.

claim: No difference in astrocyte or neuron numbers was found between TrkB.T1 KO and wildtype littermate PND 28 mice in the motor/somatosensory cortex.
source: Using Sox9 and NeuN to demarcate astrocytes and neurons respectively, we found no significant difference in the number of astrocytes or neurons in the TrkB.T1 KO mice compared to WT littermates (p>0.05; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stereological quantification shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: No significant differences in cortical thickness were found in TrkB.T1 KO mice compared to WT littermates.
source: The total and layer-specific thickness of the cortex was also assessed, and again we found no significant differences in cortical thickness in the TrkB.T1 KO mice compared to WT littermates (p>0.05; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Cortical thickness measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Publicly available RNA sequencing databases corroborate that astrocytes express the highest levels of Ntrk2 relative to other CNS cell types.
source: Publicly available RNA sequencing databases corroborate our data (Zhang et al., 2014), and, in fact, additionally demonstrate that human astrocytes express the highest levels of Ntrk2 (Kelley et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: Reference to external databases with citations to Zhang et al., 2014, Kelley et al., 2018, and Zhang et al., 2016.

claim: Human astrocytes express the highest levels of Ntrk2.
source: Publicly available RNA sequencing databases corroborate our data (Zhang et al., 2014), and, in fact, additionally demonstrate that human astrocytes express the highest levels of Ntrk2 (Kelley et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: Reference to external databases with citations to Kelley et al., 2018 and Zhang et al., 2016.

claim: TrkB.T1 has historically been presumed to act in a dominant negative capacity to prevent overactivation of BDNF signaling pathways.
source: Truncated TrkB.T1 lacks the canonical tyrosine kinase signaling domain, and therefore has historically been presumed to act in a dominant negative capacity to prevent overactivation of BDNF signaling pathways (Fenner, 2012; Klein et al., 1989; Middlemas et al., 1994).
evidence: Statement of historical interpretation with citations to Fenner, 2012, Klein et al., 1989, and Middlemas et al., 1994.

claim: In vivo dysfunction of astrocytic TrkB.T1 has been implicated in mediating neuropathic pain and motor dysfunction following spinal cord injuries.
source: Supporting this, in vivo dysfunction of astrocytic TrkB.T1 has been implicated in mediating neuropathic pain and motor dysfunction following spinal cord injuries (Matyas et al., 2017).
evidence: Citation to Matyas et al., 2017 demonstrating previous work on TrkB.T1 in astrocytes.

claim: BDNF application to cultured astrocytes resulted in a PLCγ-IP3R mediated rise in calcium with kinetics different from cultured neurons.
source: BDNF application to cultured astrocytes resulted in a PLCy-IP3R mediated rise in calcium with kinetics different from cultured neurons (Rose et al., 2003).
evidence: Citation to Rose et al., 2003 describing BDNF effects on astrocyte calcium signaling.

claim: The TrkB.T1 receptor has been found to co-immunoprecipitate with a RhoGTPase inhibitor, RhoGDIa in primary astrocyte cultures.
source: Additionally, the TrkB.T1 receptor has been found to co-immunoprecipitate with a RhoGTPase inhibitor, RhoGDIa in primary astrocyte cultures, and inhibition of RhoA increased the area occupied by cultured astrocytes (Ohira et al., 2005).
evidence: Citation to Ohira et al., 2005 describing TrkB.T1 interaction with RhoGDIa.

claim: Inhibition of RhoA increased the area occupied by cultured astrocytes.
source: Additionally, the TrkB.T1 receptor has been found to co-immunoprecipitate with a RhoGTPase inhibitor, RhoGDIa in primary astrocyte cultures, and inhibition of RhoA increased the area occupied by cultured astrocytes (Ohira et al., 2005).
evidence: Citation to Ohira et al., 2005 describing effects of RhoA inhibition on astrocyte morphology.

claim: RhoGTPases have known roles in regulating astrocytic cytoskeletal dynamics.
source: Given RhoGTPases's known roles in regulating astrocytic cytoskeletal dynamics (Zeug et al., 2018), this presents a potential mechanism by which BDNF increases astrocyte morphological complexity in astrocytes.
evidence: Citation to Zeug et al., 2018 describing RhoGTPase function in astrocytes.

claim: Time and dose dependent effects have been observed for many BDNF/TrkB.FL downstream signaling mediators, including phosphorylation of CREB, ERK, and Akt.
source: Time and dose dependent effects have been observed for many BDNF/TrkB.FL downstream signaling mediators, including phosphorylation of CREB, ERK, and Akt (Cunha et al., 2009; Jia et al., 2007; Mamounas et al., 2000), leading to alterations in neuronal cell survival, axonal sprouting, and enhancement or deficits to learning and memory behaviors (for review see Kowiański et al., 2018).
evidence: Citations to Cunha et al., 2009, Jia et al., 2007, Mamounas et al., 2000, and Kowiański et al., 2018 describing dose-dependent BDNF effects.

claim: In Drosophila, FGF signaling through the Heartless receptor determines astrocyte domain size and infiltration into the neuropil.
source: In Drosophila, FGF signaling through the Heartless receptor determines astrocyte domain size and infiltration into the neuropil (Stork et al., 2014).
evidence: Citation to Stork et al., 2014 describing FGF/Heartless signaling in Drosophila astrocytes.

claim: Pharmacological and genetic manipulations of mGluR5 in astrocytes reduced the developmental increase in astrocytic volume between PND 14 and 21.
source: Pharmacological and genetic manipulations of mGluR5 in astrocytes reduced the developmental increase in astrocytic volume between PND 14 and 21 (Morel et al., 2014).
evidence: Citation to Morel et al., 2014 describing mGluR5 effects on astrocyte morphology.

claim: Loss of neuroligins in astrocytes and/or their neuronal neurexin partner reduced astrocyte morphogenesis in the visual cortex by PND 21.
source: Similarly, loss of neuroligins in astrocytes and/or their neuronal neurexin partner reduced astrocyte morphogenesis in the visual cortex by PND 21.
evidence: Description of neuroligin/neurexin effects on astrocyte morphology, likely referencing Stogsdill et al., 2017 mentioned earlier.

claim: Global TrkB.T1 knockout animals demonstrate anxiety-like behaviors.
source: It should be noted that the global TrkB.T1 knock out animals demonstrate anxiety like behaviors (Carim-Todd et al., 2009).
evidence: Citation to Carim-Todd et al., 2009 describing behavioral phenotype of global TrkB.T1 KO mice.

claim: Previous work demonstrated no change in basal synaptic transmission or LTP in the hippocampus, but found decreased neuronal arborization in the amygdala and anxiety-like behavior in 8 week old global TrkB.T1 KO mice.
source: This is particularly interesting as previous work demonstrated no change in basal synaptic transmission or LTP in the hippocampus, but found decreased neuronal arborization in the amygdala and anxiety-like behavior in 8 week old global TrkB.T1 KO mice (Carim-Todd et al., 2009).
evidence: Citation to Carim-Todd et al., 2009 describing synaptic and behavioral phenotypes in TrkB.T1 KO mice.

claim: Increased mEPSC amplitude is associated with synaptic scaling in response to reduced activity.
source: Additionally, increased mEPSC amplitude is associated with synaptic scaling in response to reduced activity, and we demonstrate a concomitant reduction in the number of synapses and frequency of mEPSC.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about synaptic scaling mechanisms.

claim: Similar patterns of synaptic dysfunction were found in hippocampal slice mEPSCs of neurodevelopmental disorder Rett Syndrome, with right shifted cumulative probabilities in both frequency and amplitude.
source: Similar patterns of synaptic dysfunction were found in hippocampal slice mEPSCs of neurodevelopmental disorder Rett Syndrome, with right shifted cumulative probabilities in both frequency and amplitude (Calfa et al., 2015).
evidence: Citation to Calfa et al., 2015 describing synaptic dysfunction in Rett Syndrome.

claim: Aberrant BDNF expression and dysfunctional astrocytes are well characterized in Rett Syndrome.
source: Intriguingly, aberrant BDNF expression and dysfunctional astrocytes are well characterized in Rett.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about Rett Syndrome pathology.

claim: Following synaptogenesis, BDNF secretion from neurons is largely targeted to synaptic zones and is secreted in an activity-dependent manner.
source: This experiment is particularly interesting given that following synaptogenesis, BDNF secretion from neurons is largely targeted to synaptic zones and is secreted in an activity-dependent manner (Park and Poo, 2013).
evidence: Citation to Park and Poo, 2013 describing BDNF secretion patterns.

claim: siRNA knockdown of TrkB.T1 in adult rats leads to decreased ability of cortical astrocytes to modulate their morphology in response to neuronal activity.
source: One study suggests that this may indeed occur, as siRNA knockdown of TrkB.T1 in adult rats leads to decreased ability of cortical astrocytes to modulate their morphology in response to neuronal activity (Ohira et al., 2007).
evidence: Citation to Ohira et al., 2007 describing effects of TrkB.T1 knockdown on astrocyte morphology.

claim: Astrocytes actively contribute to synaptogenesis through release of astrocyte derived factors such as hevin, thrombospondins, SPARC, and glypicans 4/6.
source: Astrocytes actively contribute to synaptogenesis through release of astrocyte derived factors such as hevin (Kucukdereli et al., 2011), thrombospondins (Christopherson et al., 2005), SPARC (Kucukdereli et al., 2011), and glypicans 4/6 (Allen et al., 2012).
evidence: Citations to Kucukdereli et al., 2011, Christopherson et al., 2005, and Allen et al., 2012 describing astrocyte-derived synaptogenic factors.

claim: Astrocyte enwrapment of synapses is regulated by neuronal activity and can stabilize synapses following LTP.
source: Astrocyte enwrapment of synapses is additionally known to be regulated by neuronal activity, and can stabilize synapses following LTP (Bernardinelli et al., 2014).
evidence: Citation to Bernardinelli et al., 2014 describing activity-dependent astrocyte enwrapment.

claim: Peripheral astrocyte processes represent upwards of 85% of in vivo astrocytic volume.
source: The visualization and quantification of astrocyte membrane, which accounts for upwards of 85% of in vivo astrocytic volume, results in more physiologically relevant information.
evidence: Statement about astrocyte membrane composition, likely based on established knowledge.

claim: Glast is a membrane localized glutamate transporter highly expressed in astrocyte populations.
source: Glast—a membrane localized glutamate transporter—is highly expressed in astrocyte populations (Kondo et al., 1995) and Ezrin—a member of the ERM protein family—links the plasma membrane to the actin cytoskeleton, and has been previously demonstrated to be localized to peripheral astrocyte processes (Derouiche and Frotscher, 2001; Lavialle et al., 2011).
evidence: Citation to Kondo et al., 1995 describing Glast expression in astrocytes.

claim: Ezrin is a member of the ERM protein family that links the plasma membrane to the actin cytoskeleton and has been demonstrated to be localized to peripheral astrocyte processes.
source: Glast—a membrane localized glutamate transporter—is highly expressed in astrocyte populations (Kondo et al., 1995) and Ezrin—a member of the ERM protein family—links the plasma membrane to the actin cytoskeleton, and has been previously demonstrated to be localized to peripheral astrocyte processes (Derouiche and Frotscher, 2001; Lavialle et al., 2011).
evidence: Citations to Derouiche and Frotscher, 2001 and Lavialle et al., 2011 describing Ezrin localization in astrocytes.
